claim: Mutations within Ras proteins represent major drivers in human cancer.
source: Mutations within Ras proteins represent major drivers in human cancer.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cancer biology, supported by extensive research cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ras proteins act as key regulators of many cellular processes by switching between inactive GDP-bound and active GTP-bound states.
source: Ras proteins act as key regulators of many cellular processes by switching between inactive GDP-bound and active GTP-bound states, the latter specifically activating several downstream signalling pathways (Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cox et al., 2014, indicating established knowledge in the field.

claim: Oncogenic Ras mutations are found in about 25% of all human cancers.
source: Oncogenic Ras mutations that lead to dysregulation of the switch mechanism are found in about 25% of all human cancers, including three of the most lethal forms (lung, colon, and pancreatic cancer).
evidence: This is a cited statistic representing established knowledge in cancer research.

claim: KRas is the predominantly mutated Ras isoform at 85%.
source: Among the Ras proteins, KRas is the predominantly mutated isoform (85%), followed by NRas (11%) and HRas (4%), with mutational hotspots at amino acid positions G12, G13, and Q61 (Cox et al., 2014; Hobbs et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cox et al., 2014 and Hobbs et al., 2016.

claim: G13 is the second most common mutation site in Ras proteins, found in 14% of tumors.
source: Although the glycine at position 12 is the most commonly mutated residue, G13 is the second most common mutation (14% of tumors harbor a mutation at this position) and in 6% of these cases, an acquired cysteine is found (Forbes et al., 2015; Visscher et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Forbes et al., 2015 and Visscher et al., 2016.

claim: The prevalence of the G13C mutation in lung cancer is 3%, equivalent to approximately 7000 individuals in the US per year.
source: In lung cancer, the prevalence of the G13C mutation is 3%, which is equivalent to approximately 7000 individuals in the US per year (Forbes et al., 2015; Burge and Hobbs, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Forbes et al., 2015 and Burge and Hobbs, 2022.

claim: Ras proteins were long considered undruggable.
source: Because of their prominent role in cancer, Ras oncogenes were identified as attractive targets for cancer therapy since their initial discovery in 1981, but attempts to target Ras have been largely unsuccessful and Ras proteins were long considered undruggable.
evidence: This represents historical knowledge about Ras drug development efforts.

claim: Sotorasib was approved by the FDA in May 2021 as the first-in-class KRasG12C inhibitor for treatment of non-small-cell lung cancer.
source: In May 2021, the first-in-class KRasG12C inhibitor Sotorasib (Amgen) was approved by the FDA for the treatment of non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), confirming the therapeutic susceptibility of mutant KRas in cancer (Mullard, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mullard, 2021, documenting a specific FDA approval event.

claim: Nucleotide-based covalent inhibitors with electrophilic groups attached to the 2',3'-position of the ribose can selectively react with KRasG13C.
source: In this publication, we demonstrate that GDP/GTP/GppCp analogues with an electrophilic group attached to the ribose interact with the necessary high reversible affinity to KRas and are able to react covalently with KRasG13C.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The acrylamide nucleotide derivatives can selectively react with KRasG13C but not with KRasG12C.
source: Mass spectrometry experiments and kinetic studies reveal promising molecular properties of these covalent inhibitors
evidence: Supported by MS experiments shown in Figure 1C, D, E demonstrating selective modification of KRasG13C over KRasG12C.

claim: The eda linker led to the most efficient covalent protein modification of KRasG13C.
source: The eda linker led to the most efficient covalent protein modification (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing different linker lengths.

claim: Using dGTP analogues, the rate of covalent protein modification was further increased in the case of the eda derivative.
source: Using dGTP analogues, the rate of covalent protein modification was further increased in the case of the eda derivative, indicating that the linker in the 3'-position of the ribose is superior to the 2'-position with respect to targeting KRasG13C.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing modification rates of different nucleotide derivatives.

claim: Complete modification of KRasG13C was only observed at elevated pH.
source: Although, complete modification of KRasG13C was only observed at elevated pH, significant modification of the protein also occurred at a physiological pH within 24 hr.
evidence: Supported by pH-dependent labeling experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: GTP analogues are hydrolyzed to GDP after covalent reaction with KRasG13C.
source: On incubating KRasG13C1-169 (Cys-light) with the GTP analogues, we observed at intermediate stages a mixture of covalently bound GDP and GTP forms of KRasG13C1-169 (Cys-light), but ultimately the reaction yielded only the diphosphate form, indicating that the nucleotides were still hydrolysed after the covalent reaction and were properly positioned in the active site of KRas (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by time-resolved MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The modified nucleotides are able to compete with natural GDP/GTP.
source: Additionally, we tested whether the nucleotides were generally able to compete with their natural counterparts and monitored the reaction also in the presence of equimolar concentrations as well as 10 x and 100 x excess of GDP/GTP (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). This shows that although the reaction is slowed down due to the competing nature of GDP and GTP, the modified nucleotides are able to compete.
evidence: Supported by competition experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: For KRasWT, very little unspecific labelling was observed at pH 9.5 compared to the G13C mutant (approximately 3% at pH 9, 8% at pH 9.5).
source: For KRasWT1-169, very little unspecific labelling was observed at pH 9.5 compared to the G13C mutant (approximately 3% at pH 9, 8% at pH 9.5, whereas under equivalent conditions, KRasG13C modification was ≥90%; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 6)
evidence: Supported by MS data comparing labeling of KRasWT vs KRasG13C shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Only about 7% of Ras small GTPase superfamily members contain cysteines within the P-loop that might potentially be accessible by the linker design.
source: In addition, the multiple sequence alignment of the Ras small GTPase superfamily revealed that only about 7% of the GTPase members contain cysteines within the P-loop that might potentially be accessible by our linker design and only 3 contain Cys at the position equivalent to residue 13 in Ras (Arl4a, RheBL1, Rab21).
evidence: Supported by multiple sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Rab21 can be modified by edaGDP similarly to KRasG13C.
source: Upon incubating Rab21 with edaGDP, we indeed observed similar modification compared to KRasG13C (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: The association rate constants (kon) of the nucleotide analogues are comparable to those of unmodified nucleotides.
source: By fitting the data to a previously described model (Müller et al., 2017), we obtained the corresponding kon values, and those for the nucleotide analogues were comparable to those of the unmodified nucleotide (Table 1—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by stopped-flow experiments and kinetic analysis shown in Table 1—source data 1 and 2.

claim: The dissociation constants for pdaGDP and bdaGDP were calculated to be 8.6±1.3 pM and 9.6±0.5 pM, respectively.
source: Based on the relative abundance of bound nucleotides determined by the HPLC assay, the dissociation constants for the pda and bda derivatives were calculated to be 8.6±1.3 pM and 9.6±0.5 pM, respectively (overlap with the GDP elution peak prevented accurate determination in the case of the eda-derivative; Method section, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by HPLC-based competition experiments and calculations shown in Table 1—source data 3 and 4.

claim: The attached linker has very little impact on the reversible interaction and affinity of nucleotides to KRas.
source: Thus, the attached linker has very little impact on the reversible interaction and the affinity, an important fact that must be considered for the approach of using nucleotide-competitive inhibitors (Müller et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by affinity measurements showing KD values in the picomolar range similar to natural nucleotides.

claim: SML-8-73-1 showed a dramatic loss of reversible affinity (KD = ~140 nM).
source: In contrast, SML-8-73-1, a GDP derivative harbouring an electrophilic group on the β-phosphate showed a dramatic loss of reversible affinity (KD = ~140 nM) (Jeganathan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jeganathan et al., 2018.

claim: The first X-ray crystal structures of the oncogenic KRasG13C mutant were solved with covalently bound edaGDP (PDB 7ok3) and bdaGDP (PDB 7ok4).
source: To gain further insight into the binding mode of the covalently bound nucleotides, we solved the first X-ray crystal structure of the oncogenic KRasG13C mutant, in this case with covalently bound edaGDP (PDB 7ok3) and bdaGDP (PDB 7ok4) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by X-ray crystallography data and structures deposited in PDB.

claim: Only the 3'-isomer of the nucleotide analogues was observed in the crystal structures.
source: Interestingly, only the 3'-isomer of the nucleotide analogues was observed in the structures, consistent with results of the MS experiments comparing the efficiency of labelling of the dGTP derivative and the mixed isomers of the GTP derivative and showing a faster reaction for dGTP (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 2 and MS experiments in Figure 1C.

claim: Both crystal structures lacked Mg2+ ions in the active site despite a Mg2+ concentration of 2 mM in the Ras solution.
source: However, both structures lacked the Mg2+ ions in the active site despite a Mg2+ concentration of 2 mM in the Ras solution.
evidence: Observed in the crystal structures (PDB 7ok3 and 7ok4).

claim: The missing Mg2+-ions are probably a result of the crystallization buffer containing NH4F or NaF, leading to precipitation of poorly soluble MgF2.
source: The missing Mg2+-ions are probably a result of the crystallization buffer containing NH4F or NaF, leading to precipitation of poorly soluble MgF2, and this has also been observed in other PDB-deposited structures presumably because of similar effects of the reservoir solutions used in the crystallization process (e.g. PDB 4m1o, 4lyf, 4lyh, 4m21, 4m1s, 4m1t, 4m1t, 4m1y) (Ostrem et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on crystallization conditions and comparison with other structures, supported by citation to Ostrem et al., 2013.

claim: SOS was unable to catalyze nucleotide exchange on covalently locked KRasG13C-edaGDP.
source: Whereas SOS efficiently catalysed nucleotide exchange on KRasWT, KRasG13C and as a control on KRasG13C:acetyledaGDP, it was unable to do so with the covalently locked G13C-edaGDP mutant, showing that the protein is indeed locked in the inactive state (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by GEF-catalyzed nucleotide exchange experiments shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: KRasG13C shows a drastically increased intrinsic nucleotide exchange rate compared to KRasWT in the absence of SOS.
source: Interestingly, in these experiments we also observed a drastically increased intrinsic nucleotide exchange rate for KRasG13C compared to KRasWT in the absence of SOS (Figure 3A, blue area), an effect that probably contributes to the increased signalling and oncogenic effect of this mutant, and also this effect is abrogated in the case of covalently locked KRasG13C-edaGDP (Hunter et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by nucleotide exchange experiments shown in Figure 3A and citation to Hunter et al., 2015.

claim: No SOS-catalysed nucleotide exchange was observed for covalently modified KRasG13C-edaGppCp.
source: Similarly, no SOS-catalysed nucleotide exchange was observed in case of covalently modified KRasG13C-edaGppCp, indicating that the protein can also be trapped in the active conformation with the corresponding nucleoside-triphosphates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The intrinsic GTP hydrolysis of KRasG13C-edaGTP (t1/2 = 187 min) is comparable to that of KRasWT:GTP (t1/2 = 126 min).
source: While the intrinsic GTP hydrolysis of KRasG13C-edaGTP (t1/2 = 187 min) is comparable to that of KRasWT:GTP (t1/2 = 126 min) and even faster than for the KRasG12C mutant (t1/2 = 300 min) (Li et al., 2021; Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by GTP hydrolysis experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to Li et al., 2021.

claim: A drastically decreased GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis was observed for the KRasG13C mutant.
source: a drastically decreased GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis was observed for the G13C mutant as expected (Scheffzek et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by GAP-stimulated hydrolysis experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to Scheffzek et al., 1997.

claim: Covalently locked KRasG13C can still be fully farnesylated in vitro.
source: Importantly, we confirmed that the covalently locked protein can still be fully farnesylated in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Supported by in vitro farnesylation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: MS/MS analysis revealed selective labelling of the targeted cysteine residue at position 13 in full-length KRasG13C.
source: and the covalent modification of full-length KRasG13C was further validated through MS/MS‐analysis, which revealed selective labelling of the targeted cysteine residue at position 13 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Electroporation of KRasG13C into HeLa cells resulted in concentration-dependent activation of downstream signaling (pcRaf, pAkt, pErk, and pS6).
source: However, whereas we observed a concentration-dependent activation of the downstream signalling and upregulation of pcRaf, pAkt, pErk, and pS6 upon delivery of KRasG13C, the covalently locked variant was unable to induce these effects and, similarly to KRasWT, no increase in downstream signalling was observed (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3B, C and Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7.

claim: Covalently locked KRasG13C-edaGDP was unable to induce oncogenic signaling in cells.
source: However, whereas we observed a concentration-dependent activation of the downstream signalling and upregulation of pcRaf, pAkt, pErk, and pS6 upon delivery of KRasG13C, the covalently locked variant was unable to induce these effects and, similarly to KRasWT, no increase in downstream signalling was observed (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3B, C and Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7.

claim: Electroporation of non-covalently modified KRasG13C:acetyledaGDP resulted in activation of the Ras pathway comparable to KRasG13C.
source: In addition, upon electroporation of non-covalently modified KRasG13C:acetyledaGDP or covalently modified KRasG13C-edaGppCP, activation of the Ras pathway comparable to KRasG13C was observed, showing that covalent modification is essential for inhibition of oncogenic signalling
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claim: Covalent modification is essential for inhibition of oncogenic signaling by nucleotide analogues.
source: showing that covalent modification is essential for inhibition of oncogenic signalling
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of covalently modified vs non-covalently modified nucleotide analogues in cellular experiments.

claim: Covalently modified KRasG13C-edaGppCp can artificially activate the Ras pathway.
source: and that artificial activation can be induced using non-hydrolysable GTP derivatives, which potentially adds further possibilities of using these nucleotide analogues to study Ras biology (Figure 3—figure supplements 8 and 9).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 9.

claim: KRasG13C is a frequently observed mutation in cancer.
source: In summary, we have successfully developed nucleotide-based covalent inhibitors of oncogenic KRasG13C, a variant of KRas that is largely unexplored as a target even though it is a frequently observed mutation in cancer (Visscher et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Visscher et al., 2016.

claim: The nucleotide analogues have similar affinities towards Ras compared to their natural counterparts.
source: Thorough biochemical and structural characterization revealed that the nucleotide analogues designed and synthesized in this publication have similar affinities towards Ras compared to their natural counterparts.
evidence: Supported by affinity measurements showing KD values in the picomolar range (Table 1).

claim: The nucleotides prohibit SOS-mediated nucleotide exchange.
source: We could show that the nucleotides prohibit (SOS-mediated) nucleotide exchange and lead to an effective interference in the induction of oncogenic effects by KRasG13C in living cells.
evidence: Supported by GEF assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The nucleotides lead to effective interference in the induction of oncogenic effects by KRasG13C in living cells.
source: We could show that the nucleotides prohibit (SOS-mediated) nucleotide exchange and lead to an effective interference in the induction of oncogenic effects by KRasG13C in living cells.
evidence: Supported by cellular experiments shown in Figure 3B, C.

claim: Further optimization of the nucleotides to overcome limitations regarding reactivity at physiological pH and cell-permeability are necessary and currently ongoing.
source: Further optimization of the nucleotides to overcome the limitations regarding reactivity at physiological pH, as well as cell-permeability, are necessary and currently ongoing.
evidence: This is a statement about future work and current limitations.

claim: Protective esterification of the diphosphate moiety is being investigated to deliver prodrugs of the nucleotides into cells.
source: Additionally, protective esterification of the diphosphate moiety is currently being investigated to deliver prodrugs of the nucleotides into cells, which subsequently become activated by unspecific esterases (Meier, 2017; Mehellou et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes ongoing research efforts, supported by citations to Meier, 2017 and Mehellou et al., 2018.

claim: Appropriate modification of the linker length and electrophilic warhead could make KRasG12C or other relevant mutants possible targets.
source: We are also investigating whether appropriate modification of the linker length and the electrophilic warhead would also make KRasG12C or other relevant mutants (e.g. HRasG12S in Costello syndrome) (Gripp and Lin, 2012) a possible target in a similar approach.
evidence: This describes future research directions, supported by citation to Gripp and Lin, 2012.

claim: The G13C mutation should be generally addressable by appropriately positioned Michael acceptors based on pKa calculations.
source: However, based on pKa calculations, we were able to show that the G13C mutation should also be generally addressable by appropriately positioned Michael acceptors (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by pKa calculations shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Modifications at the 2',3'-OH groups of the ribose do not significantly alter nucleotide affinity.
source: In contrast to Gray and colleagues, we chose the 2',3'-OH groups of the ribose for attachment of the warhead since modifications at this position do not significantly alter nucleotide affinity (Figure 1A, B; Eberth et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Eberth et al., 2005 and experimental data in this study.

claim: The warhead reacts preferentially with the cysteine at position 13, but not other cysteines in KRas nor the additional neighboring cysteine in KRasG12C.
source: thus showing that the warhead reacts preferentially with the cysteine at position 13, but not other cysteines in KRas nor the additional neighboring cysteine in KRasG12C.
evidence: Supported by MS experiments comparing labeling of KRasG13C, KRasG12C, and KRasWT shown in Figure 1.

claim: Knock-down of Rab21 has been reported to have beneficial effects in human glioma cells.
source: In fact, Rab21 might be an interesting target itself since knock-down of Rab21 has been reported to have beneficial effects in human glioma cells (Ge et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ge et al., 2017.

claim: Position 12 is further remote compared to position 13 from the ribose OH-groups, explaining the observed specificity of covalent bond formation.
source: (B) Model of KRasG13C (model is based on PDB 4obe) showing the distances between the cysteine residue and the OH-groups of the ribose and the general structure of nucleotide derivatives bearing an electrophilic group at the 2',3'-position of the ribose moiety, showing that position 12 is further remote compared to position 13 and thus explaining the observed specificity of covalent bond formation.
evidence: Supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The overall structures of KRasG13C-edaGDP and KRasG13C-bdaGDP are very similar to the known structure of KRas:GDP (PDB 4obe).
source: The overall structures are very similar to the known structure of KRas:GDP (PDB 4obe), and the nucleotide scaffold, as well as the covalent linkage for both nucleotide analogues with cysteine at position 13 are well resolved in the electron density (Figure 2C, E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The nucleotides are bound within the active site in a manner comparable to non-covalently bound GDP in other structures of Ras.
source: Both structures showed that the nucleotides are bound within the active site in a manner that is comparable to non-covalently bound GDP in other structures of Ras, with similar reversible interactions between the protein and the nucleotide and the additional well-resolved covalent link to Cys13.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2.

claim: The eda and bda linkers are remote from the Mg2+ binding site and do not directly interfere with Mg2+ binding.
source: In both crystal structures, the eda and bda linker are remote from the Mg2+ binding site and do not directly interfere with Mg2+ binding, suggesting that Mg2+ can generally bind.
evidence: Supported by structural analysis of crystal structures (PDB 7ok3 and 7ok4).

claim: The structural analysis verified the nucleotide binding pose and the high reversible affinity comparable to the natural nucleotides.
source: Thus, the structural analysis verified the nucleotide binding pose and the high reversible affinity comparable to the natural nucleotides and will guide design and optimisation of the linker and the warhead in further studies.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the crystallographic and biochemical data presented.

claim: KRasG13C shows drastically increased intrinsic nucleotide exchange rate compared to KRasWT, which probably contributes to the increased signalling and oncogenic effect of this mutant.
source: Interestingly, in these experiments we also observed a drastically increased intrinsic nucleotide exchange rate for KRasG13C compared to KRasWT in the absence of SOS (Figure 3A, blue area), an effect that probably contributes to the increased signalling and oncogenic effect of this mutant
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3A and inference about biological significance, with citation to Hunter et al., 2015.

claim: GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis requires equivalent amounts of GAP (GAP 1:1) for KRasG13C-edaGTP (t1/2 = 35 min), while KRasWT:GTP requires only catalytic amounts (GAP 1:1000, t1/2 = 16 min).
source: While GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis can be observed for KRasWT:GTP already at catalytic amounts of GAP (GAP 1:1000, t1/2 = 16 min), KRasG13C-edaGTP requires equivalent amounts of GAP (GAP 1:1, t1/2 = 35 min).
evidence: Supported by GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: HeLa cells were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC).
source: HeLa cells were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and were cultured in DMEM medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (PAN-Biotech) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Gibco).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about cell line source.

claim: The identity of the cells was validated by STR profiling and the cells were tested negative for mycoplasma contamination.
source: The identity of the cells was validated by STR profiling and the cells were tested negative for mycoplasma contamination.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about cell line authentication.
